To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the wood-decay fungi differ in the production of extracellular oxidases and that this pattern correlates to their ecophysiological behaviour and taxonomy.
the activity of ligninolytic peroxideases correlates with the degradation of lignin, whereas laccase activity correlates with the formation of water-soluble lignin fragments.
the degradation of lignocelullulose and the production of lignin-degrading enzymes by fungi are highly dependent on their taxonomic and ecophysiological group.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the elucidation of the role of the oxidative enzymes in the degradation of lignin and lignin-related compounds and in the formation of water-soluble low-molecular mass compounds and high-molecular mass lignin fragments during wood decay.
the elucidation of the role of different oxidative enzymes during the decay of wood and litter.
the elucidation of the role of different fungal ligninolytic systems in wood decay and the development of a method for the detection of wood-rotting fungi in nature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the degradation of lignocelulose and the production of oxidoreductases are not a unique feature of the basidiomycete white rot fungi but also a characteristic of some ascomycetes.

the ligninolytic peroxides of basidiomycete fungi play a major role in wood degradation, whereas laccases are of minor importance, but they may be involved in the formation of high molecular mass lignin degradation products.

the ligninolytic potential of fungi is not restricted to the classic lignin peroxidases and manganese peroxidase, and that the role of laccases and novel peroxidases in wood decay is not yet understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the white-rot fungus Phlebia radiate was able to degrade beechwood lignocellulosic material and release a large amount of small water-solu-ble fragments (0.1-1 kDa) containing aromatic constituents.

the white rotters of wood and leaf litter (Phlebia radiata and Stropharia rugoso-annulata, respectively) showed the highest ligninolytic potential, while the ascomycete Xylaria polymorphus caused a soft rot of wood.
the degradation of beech-wood is mainly caused by manganese-oxidizing lignin peroxidases and that the role of laccases is limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ligninolytic peroxides of basidiomycetous fungi are not only the key players in lignocellulolytic degradation but they are also the main source of aromatic metabolites in the environment.

ligninolytic peroxidasessuch as manganese peroxidases, aromatic peroxygenases and the recently discovered manganese-independent peroxidases of the DyP type - play a key role in the degradation of lignin in beech wood.
different fungi use different enzymes and enzyme combinations to degrade wood, and that these enzyme combinations can be used to distinguish the rot type.
